title: Reliable Neighborhood-Aware Multi-View Outlier Detection
claim: Outliers come in distinct types defined by how far they sit from neighbors and whether neighborhoods differ across views.
layout: 2 panels (View 1, View 2) side by side, legend below, dashed neighbor links
description: The figure sits inside a large dotted rounded frame labeled K=3, split into two dotted sub-panels, View 1 on the left and View 2 on the right. Each panel is a 2-D scatter of the same instances, drawn as open black circles and open blue triangles that form two clusters. Three highlighted outliers appear in both views. A red square is the attribute outlier, an orange diamond is the class outlier, and a green star is the attribute-class outlier. Long light-gray dashed lines link the red square and the green star to their distant neighbors. Short dark dashed lines link the orange diamond to its different neighbors, which belong to another cluster in the other view. Text labels read 'Distant neighbors' and 'Different neighbors'. A legend along the bottom maps the three symbols to the outlier types. The eye goes first to the red square and the star.
caption: Description of Neighborhood-based outlier definitions: Attribute outlier (red) indicates instances that are remarkably distant from its neighbors within each view. Class outlier (orange) indicates instances with remarkably different neighborhood structures across views. Attribute-Class outlier (green) exhibits characteristics of both attribute outlier and class outlier.
abstract: In recent years, multi-view outlier detection (MVOD) has gained increasing attention, with the primary objective of recovering the underlying structure of normal data from outlier-contaminated multi-view datasets. However, this objective is hindered by two fundamental challenges:(i) outlier propagation, (ii) scale discrepancy. To address these issues, we propose RNAMOD (Reliable Neighborhood-Aware Multi-View Outlier Detection), which introduces the concept of reliability and constructs a reliable neighborhood structure to avoid outlier propagation. We introduce a leave-one-out directional consensus mechanism to align cross-view neighborhood structures while preventing scale discrepancy by aligning geometric directions that remain invariant to scaling. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that RNAMOD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
